name: Hassan Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Hassan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of two buyers at Calder Building Supplies. We're a distributor that sells timber, plasterboard, insulation and fixings to builders' merchants and bigger contractors. Mornings I go through stock and the order book, then I'm on to the timber mills and the screw and bolt importers. Afternoons it's chasing late lorries and haggling, because timber prices jump around like nothing else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is getting a good price on a big load before the market moves, that's a proper buzz. What wears me down is the chasing. Half my week is emails asking where a delivery is. I use one of those AI assistants now and then to draft the chasers, but only since my colleague Gemma showed me it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Sounds plausible, to be fair. Lots of things get hyped and then just become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, well, at least the email chasing got quicker. To my mates at five-a-side I'd say it's like those smart fridges, it was supposed to change everything. I don't really post online, maybe I'd share a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think, good, my job is safe and I can keep building. I own a one-bed flat with a small mortgage, I've got savings, and I'm paid on the high side for a buyer. Nothing in that picture shakes any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the AI for chasers and price summaries, the stuff it's actually good at. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage by two hundred a month like I've been doing. Maybe I'd ask Mr Calder for a pay review once the timber market settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay review. Is your pay a worry at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really a worry. It's more that I'd like to be paid like a senior buyer one day. In this picture that happens the old way, years in and a good record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Timber prices, always. A bad year in construction hits a timber buyer hard, and that's the risk in my job, not computers. When the housebuilders paused three years ago we had yards full of joists.

say: I'd say at least **email chasing** got quicker.
I'd tell my mates AI was like **smart fridges**, hyped then ordinary.
think: My **job is safe**, so I can keep building my life.
A **small mortgage**, savings and good pay mean nothing here shakes me.
do: Use the AI for **chasers** and price summaries only.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** by two hundred a month.
Ask the owner for a **pay review** once timber settles.
S0.quote: A bad year in construction hits a timber buyer hard, and that's the risk in my job, not computers.
fieldNote: Hassan's security rests on **owning a flat** and steady pay, not on technology.
His real risk is the **construction cycle**, which he remembers clearly.
He adopted AI only after a **colleague proved it**, which fits his steady style.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for delivery chasers and price summaries
Overpay the flat mortgage by two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying's right there on the card. Hm. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to get ahead of it and pick the right system before a competitor does. To friends I'd say my job's going to look different, not disappear. I'd keep it measured, I don't like doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Calder is small and old-fashioned, and the owner likes people. I think he'd use AI to sell more without hiring, not to sack Gemma or me. But I'd have to get good at it, because a buyer who can't use the system will look slow next to one who can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until Gemma or someone at another distributor shows what works, then learn that properly, probably within six months. I'd ask Mr Calder to pay for a short course on the stock planning software we'd end up using. And I'd keep my savings where they are, no big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job feels safe for now, but the ground's moving and I'd be watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner likes people. What if he retired or sold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that bothers me. Mr Calder is sixty-four. If a bigger group bought out my small firm, they'd run the buying from head office with AI and I'd be gone. I try not to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Gemma keeps coming up. How do you two compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma's quicker with new stuff than me, she'd be fine. I'm better with the mills, I know the people. In this picture I think both of those still matter for a few years.

say: I'd urge the firm to **pick a system** before competitors do.
I'd tell friends my job will **look different**, not disappear.
think: The owner would use AI to **grow without hiring**, not to sack us.
A buyer who **can't use the system** will look slow next to one who can.
do: Wait for **proven tools**, then learn them properly within six months.
Ask the owner to fund a short **stock planning course**.
Keep savings where they are with **no big moves**.
feel: **Uneasy**, safe for now but watching the **ground move**.
S1.quote: If a bigger group bought out my small firm, they'd run the buying from head office with AI and I'd be gone.
fieldNote: Hassan feels safe because of a **people-minded owner** at a small firm.
His hidden worry is a **takeover**, since the owner is sixty-four.
He'll learn AI **after others prove it**, in about six months.

steps.text: Learn the chosen stock planning software once Gemma has tested it
Ask the owner to pay for a short stock planning course
Hold off on big money moves and watch the owner's plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Bloody hell. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be talking to every customer now about what they'll still need from us. To friends I'd say nobody's ready, not the firms, not the government. I'd probably share a few articles, the sensible ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying is gone by 2028. The lorries, the yard and the forklifts carry on till about 2031 because those are hands-on. Builders still want a person on site to sort out a short delivery. I'd have about nine months of savings plus the flat, so I wouldn't starve, but I'd be out of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and put that money into savings instead, cash I can reach. Second, I'd ask Mr Calder about moving into a site sales role, visiting contractors, because that's face to face. I'd cancel the car upgrade I'd been planning. And I'd start applying for rep jobs at the bigger merchants by month three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel it in my stomach. I've got cushion, but two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said site sales is face to face. Isn't selling also thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes, the quotes and the pricing would go to AI. But a robot isn't standing on a muddy site with a furious foreman about a missing pallet of blocks before 2031. That's my three-year gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum and Dad I've got a plan and the flat's safe. My dad would say get into a trade, he's an electrician. Maybe he's right, honestly.

say: I'd say we should ask **every customer** now what they'll still need.
I'd tell friends **nobody's ready**, not firms or government.
think: **Buying is gone** by 2028, but yard and lorry work lasts till 2031.
Nine months' savings and **the flat** mean I won't starve, but I'd lose the job.
do: Stop overpaying the mortgage and build **cash savings** instead.
Ask about a **site sales role** and apply for rep jobs by month three.
feel: **Anxious**, a feeling in my **stomach**, because two years is nothing.
S2.quote: A robot isn't standing on a muddy site with a furious foreman about a missing pallet of blocks before 2031.
fieldNote: Hassan uses the **three-year robot gap** to aim at site sales.
His **savings and flat** give him a sense of control despite expecting job loss.
His electrician dad's advice about **getting into a trade** lands with him.

steps.text: Redirect the mortgage overpayment into an instant-access savings account
Apply for site sales rep jobs at bigger builders' merchants
Cancel the planned car upgrade this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the thinking stuff, 2034 for the robots. Five years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this gives us time to do it right. To friends I'd say I'm going to be one of those people with a plan B, finally. I'd keep the online stuff to a minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job still ends, just in 2031. That's five years to get myself into the part of the building trade that's hands-on or on site. I'm not as quick with tech as Gemma, but I'm not stupid either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the AI buying tools properly, because doing the job well for five years still matters for my pay and references. I'd look into a site supervisor course, maybe two evenings a week. And I'd think about renting out the flat if I needed to move nearer the big contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like I'd have a to-do list instead of a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's an electrician. Have you thought about that route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, maybe. An electrician's apprenticeship at twenty-eight is a bit late but people do it. The robots for that kind of work come later, maybe even later than 2034, wiring old houses is messy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI tools and also leave buying. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd learn the tools to do the job well while it lasts and keep my references strong. Leaving the buying job in year four with a good name is better than being pushed out in year five.

say: I'd say five years gives the firm **time** to do it right.
I'd tell friends I'll finally have a **plan B**.
think: My buying job **still ends**, just in 2031.
Five years is enough to move into **on-site building work**.
do: Learn the **AI buying tools** properly to keep my references strong.
Take a **site supervisor course** two evenings a week.
Consider **renting out the flat** to move nearer the contractors.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, with a **to-do list** instead of a knot.
S3.quote: Leaving the buying job in year four with a good name is better than being pushed out in year five.
fieldNote: Hassan sees **no contradiction** in learning AI while planning to leave buying.
He seriously considers his dad's **electrician route** with five years' warning.
The flat becomes a **possible income** if he moves for work.

steps.text: Learn Calder's AI stock buying tools properly this year
Start a site supervisor course two evenings a week
Price up renting out the flat if work moves away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and then 2039. Okay, that's a whole other conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to get caught out. With friends I'd be pretty relaxed about it. Online, nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough time for a proper change, maybe even an apprenticeship with Dad. I'd be thirty-seven when buying ends, and I'd want a trade or a site job well before that. The danger is me drifting, because I'm steady, I like things to be proven first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on buying and keep overpaying the mortgage, so the flat's nearly paid off by the time it lands. I'd do the site supervisor course in year two or three, once I see which roles are holding up. And I'd watch what Gemma does, she'll move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's fine for me, I think, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger is drifting. What would stop you drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the calendar, honestly. If I wrote down that I start the course in September 2028, I'd do it. Without a date in the calendar I'd still be buying timber in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to settle down, meet someone, all that. Ten years makes that feel normal, like any other life. Two years would make me hold everything.

say: I'd say **nobody has an excuse** to get caught out.
I'd be pretty **relaxed** about it with friends.
think: Ten years allows a **proper change**, maybe an apprenticeship with Dad.
My real risk is **drifting**, because I like things proven first.
do: Keep buying and **overpaying the mortgage** so the flat is nearly paid off.
Take the **site supervisor course** in year two or three.
Write a **start date** in the calendar to stop drifting.
feel: **Uneasy**, fine for me but **there** in the background.
S4.quote: Without a date in the calendar I'd still be buying timber in 2035.
fieldNote: Hassan knows his **steady nature** risks him drifting with a long warning.
He wants to **pay off the flat** before buying ends.
Ten years lets him keep **normal life plans** like settling down.

steps.text: Keep overpaying the mortgage so the flat is nearly paid off
Book the site supervisor course for September 2028
Watch what Gemma and other buyers do before switching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too fast for someone like me who waits to see what works. What would help is employers being made to give proper notice and pay for retraining, like a year's warning and a course paid for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the mills. The timber mills I buy from have families working there for generations, and the people on the other end of my phone calls are changing too. It's not only my job.

headlineQuote: The timber mills I buy from have families working there for generations, and the people on the other end of my phone calls are changing too.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old timber buyer** at a small, old-fashioned building supplies distributor.
He owns a **one-bed flat**, has savings and fears construction slumps more than computers.
He adopts AI **once others prove it**, often following his colleague Gemma.
He feels calm or uneasy in slower scenarios, and **anxious** when AGI comes in two or five years.
He aims for **site sales or trades**, using the three-year robot gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast for someone who waits to see what works.
whatWouldHelp: Employers giving **a year's notice** and paying for **retraining**.
